Drugs Acting on the Urinary System

Urinary drugs - diuretics, urinary antiseptics, drugs for urinary retention and BPH - uses and nursing care.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • List urinary drug classes and examples
  • Describe diuretics and their uses
  • Explain nurse responsibilities in urinary drug administration

In simple terms

Urinary system drugs treat conditions of the kidneys and bladder - fluid overload, hypertension, urinary tract infections, urinary retention and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Nurses monitor output, electrolytes and blood pressure when giving these drugs.

Common urinary drugs

Class Examples Use
Loop diuretics Furosemide, bumetanide Heart failure, oedema, hypertension
Thiazide diuretics Hydrochlorothiazide Hypertension, mild oedema
Potassium-sparing diuretics Spironolactone, amiloride Retain potassium; heart failure, ascites
Urinary antiseptics Nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Urinary analgesics Phenazopyridine Urinary pain relief (symptomatic)
Alpha-blockers Tamsulosin, terazosin Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) - urine flow
5-alpha reductase inhibitors Finasteride BPH - shrink prostate

Diuretics

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) - act on loop of Henle; powerful; cause potassium loss (hypokalaemia); monitor potassium and blood pressure
  • Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide) - mild; hypertension; cause potassium loss
  • Potassium-sparing (spironolactone, amiloride) - retain potassium; used with other diuretics to prevent hypokalaemia; monitor for hyperkalaemia

Nursing care

  • Diuretics - give in the morning (avoid night-time urination); monitor blood pressure, electrolytes (potassium), weight, urine output
  • Urinary antiseptics - nitrofurantoin for UTI; take with food; complete the course; report dark urine (harmless discolouration from nitrofurantoin)
  • Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) - first dose may cause postural hypotension; advise rising slowly; take at bedtime initially
  • Urinary retention - monitor for inability to void; report to doctor (may need catheterisation)

🔴 Diuretic timing

Give oral diuretics in the morning so the patient passes urine during the day and can sleep at night (avoid nocturia and falls).

Where the nurse uses this

  • Diuretic administration - give in the morning; monitor blood pressure, electrolytes (potassium), weight, urine output
  • Urinary antiseptics - nitrofurantoin for UTI; take with food; complete the course; report dark urine (harmless discolouration from nitrofurantoin)
  • Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) - first dose may cause postural hypotension; advise rising slowly; take at bedtime initially
  • Urinary retention - monitor for inability to void; report to doctor (may need catheterisation)

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Loop diuretics (furosemide) - heart failure, oedema, hypertension; cause potassium loss.
  2. Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide) - hypertension, mild oedema.
  3. Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride) - retain potassium.
  4. Urinary antiseptics (nitrofurantoin) - urinary tract infection.
  5. Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) - benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) - improve urine flow.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Give diuretics in the morning to avoid nocturia.
  2. Monitor blood pressure, electrolytes (potassium), weight, urine output with diuretics.
  3. Nitrofurantoin: take with food; complete course; dark urine is harmless.
  4. Alpha-blockers: first dose may cause postural hypotension; advise rising slowly.
  5. Monitor urinary retention - inability to void may need catheterisation.

📌 Memory trick

Diuretic timing: Morning pill, dry night - give diuretics in the morning so the patient sleeps dry at night.

60-second revision

  • Urinary drugs: diuretics, urinary antiseptics, alpha-blockers.
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) - oedema, HF, HTN; cause potassium loss.
  • Thiazides - hypertension; potassium-sparing - retain potassium.
  • Nitrofurantoin - UTI; with food; complete course.
  • Tamsulosin - BPH; first-dose postural hypotension.
  • Diuretics in the morning; monitor BP, potassium, weight, output.

Test yourself

Furosemide is a:

Answer: B. Furosemide is a loop diuretic - powerful, acts on the loop of Henle.

Diuretics are best given in the:

Answer: B. Diuretics are given in the morning so the patient passes urine during the day and can sleep at night.

Nitrofurantoin is used for:

Answer: B. Nitrofurantoin is a urinary antiseptic used for urinary tract infections.

Tamsulosin is used for:

Answer: B. Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) to improve urine flow.

First-dose alpha-blocker effect:

Answer: B. First-dose alpha-blocker effect may cause postural hypotension (dizziness on standing); advise rising slowly.
